planting.note: Set out container stock in fall or winter on a rocky or gravelly slope in excellent drainage; this is one of the few North American ashes with true white petals, and it needs no summer water once rooted in.

directions: California ash is a multi-stemmed, drought-deciduous shrub to small tree found in rocky canyons and on the dry margins of blue oak woodland throughout the Sierra foothills and inner Coast Ranges, usually tucked into partial shade where it gets a break from the harshest afternoon sun. Unlike most ash species, which have reduced, petal-less flowers, its early spring blooms carry small but distinct white petals in loose clusters, making it conspicuous against bare winter branches. It tolerates thin, rocky, or decomposed-granite soils and needs no irrigation beyond the first year or two of establishment. Useful as an understory or canyon-edge planting in a foothill woodland restoration where a small deciduous accent tree is wanted beneath or beside larger oaks and pines.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall on a grassy, open slope with good drainage; keep well away from vegetable beds, pasture, or anywhere grazing animals could reach it, since every part is highly toxic.

directions: Fremont's star lily sends up a basal clump of narrow leaves in late winter, followed by a sturdy spike of relatively large, creamy white, star-shaped flowers held well above the grass in the foothill meadows and open oak woodland where it grows alongside lupines and poppies from February into April. It thrives on the same lean, rocky-to-clay soils and hands-off summer dry-down that favor blue oak and its grassland associates, going fully dormant once the rains stop. All parts of the plant, including the bulb, contain potent neurotoxic alkaloids, so it is grown strictly as an ornamental or restoration subject and should never be planted where grazing animals or children could mistake it for an edible bulb. A good choice for naturalistic foothill wildflower plantings where its early, showy bloom extends the display after the small spring annuals have finished.

planting.note: Plant large, fiber-coated bulbs with the neck just at the soil surface in fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants need no summer water and resent heavy, wet ground.

directions: Soap plant forms a rosette of long, wavy-margined basal leaves at ground level, from which a tall, airy, branching flower stalk rises in early summer bearing small white, pink-veined flowers that open only in late afternoon and wither by the next morning. It is a familiar presence on the dry, grassy, often rocky foothill slopes around blue oak and valley oak woodland throughout California, where the bulb's fibrous outer coat helps it survive baked, cracked summer clay. Indigenous Californians made extensive practical use of the bulb, crushing it for a lathering soap substitute and as a fish stupefacient, and roasting it as a food source, a history worth noting alongside its garden value. In the landscape it earns a spot in dry native meadows and oak-woodland understories where its sculptural leaves and unusual twilight flowering add seasonal interest after the main spring wildflower flush fades.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; seed benefits from winter cold and moisture to break dormancy ahead of spring growth, matching its natural foothill grassland cycle.

directions: Foothill larkspur sends up slender flowering stalks topped with loose spikes of deep blue-purple, spurred flowers each spring, rising out of the grass on open slopes and in the scattered shade of blue oak and gray pine woodland across the Sierra foothills and inner Coast Ranges. Like most native larkspurs it completes its visible growth cycle quickly, flowering while the soil is still moist from winter rain and then dying back to a dormant rootstock as the ground dries out for summer. As with other Delphinium species, all parts are toxic if ingested and it should be kept away from grazing livestock. It pairs naturally with sky lupine, blue dicks, and California poppy in a foothill wildflower meadow planting, adding blue-purple vertical accents to a palette that otherwise leans toward yellow and orange.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into well-drained soil on a grassy slope in full sun to light shade; winter rain and cold handle germination without any special treatment.

directions: Purple sanicle is a low, ferny-leaved perennial in the carrot family that stands out among California foothill wildflowers for its unusual color — tight umbels of deep maroon-purple to dull red flowers held just above finely divided, pinnatifid foliage. It turns up in grassland and along the open edges of blue oak and foothill pine woodland each spring, often among the same drying clay and rocky soils that support purple needlegrass and foothill lupines. The plant goes dormant with the onset of summer drought, resprouting from a woody rootstock with the first fall rains. Though subtle rather than showy, it adds genuine color and textural variety to a native foothill meadow planting and is a good companion plant along partially shaded woodland margins where many showier annuals thin out.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in fall or winter on a partly shaded canyon slope or woodland edge in well-drained soil; established plants need little to no summer water.

directions: California snowdrop bush is a loosely branched, deciduous shrub of canyon bottoms and shaded foothill slopes within and below the blue oak woodland belt, long treated as part of the Mediterranean Styrax officinalis but now recognized by Jepson eFlora as its own distinct California species. In spring it hangs clusters of fragrant, bell-shaped white flowers with a central boss of yellow stamens along its bare or newly leafing stems, resembling a larger, woodier snowdrop. Because it is adapted to seasonal shade from oaks and other canopy trees, it performs best with some protection from the hottest afternoon sun rather than in fully open ground. It makes an attractive understory shrub for a dry, naturalistic woodland garden where its spring flower display and open branching habit can be appreciated beneath taller native trees.

planting.note: Plant bulbs from a reputable native-bulb specialist in fall, 3-4 inches deep in heavy clay or adobe-type soil in full sun to light shade; never collect from wild populations, as this species is uncommon and sensitive in much of its range.

directions: Adobe lily is an uncommon, localized bulb of the inner north Coast Range and northern Sacramento Valley foothills, favoring the heavy, cracking adobe-clay grasslands that occur in and around blue oak woodland rather than the rocky or sandy soils typical of many other foothill natives. In late winter to early spring it sends up a short stem of narrow leaves topped by several nodding, bell-shaped flowers in dusky pink to magenta tones, a color unusual among the native fritillarias. Because wild populations are limited and considered a conservation concern in parts of its range, garden stock should always come from bulbs propagated by specialty native-plant nurseries rather than field collection. It is best suited to a dedicated bulb bed or raised planting that replicates its clay-soil, winter-wet-summer-dry cycle rather than a typical well-drained rock garden.
sources: California Native Plant Society Rare Plant Program

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall, 3-4 inches deep, into heavy clay-loam or adobe soil in full sun; this grassland species tolerates the same winter-wet, summer-baked clay that supports purple needlegrass and other valley and foothill grassland natives.

directions: Stinkbells is a modest, clay-grassland native fritillary found scattered through the Central Valley margins and surrounding foothill grassland and open blue oak woodland, producing a short stem of narrow leaves and a few greenish, purple-mottled, bell-shaped flowers in early spring. The common name refers to an unpleasant, carrion-like scent the flowers give off, which attracts flies and beetles rather than bees as pollinators, an uncommon pollination strategy among California native bulbs. It is not a showy garden plant in the conventional sense but has real value in a true grassland or foothill-woodland restoration planting aiming for ecological authenticity rather than maximum color impact. Give it the same clay-heavy, summer-dry conditions it experiences in the wild and keep it away from the house if the odor during bloom is a concern.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall on a sunny or lightly shaded slope with good drainage; the corms multiply over time and need no water through their summer dormancy.

directions: Wild hyacinth produces a tight, rounded cluster of deep violet-purple flowers atop a slender, leafless stalk each late spring, distinguished from its close relative blue dicks by flowers that stay mostly closed in a dense, urn-like head rather than opening fully. It grows on grassy slopes and under the light, dappled shade of blue oak and black oak woodland through the Sierra Nevada foothills and northern Coast Ranges, where the corms sit dormant underground through the long summer dry season. Established colonies increase steadily from offset corms, making it a good choice for naturalizing in a foothill meadow or oak-woodland understory planting. It combines well with other spring foothill bulbs such as blue dicks and mariposa lilies for an extended native bloom sequence.
